title: Burden of Proof in SR&ED Claims - Canadian Tax Glossary
description: Find out why the Burden of Proof rests on the claimant to substantiate R&D eligibility and costs in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: In Canada's federal SR&ED program, the burden of proof rests on the taxpayer: claimants must adduce evidence that eligible scientific research, including testing, was undertaken. Contemporaneous documentation remains the primary evidentiary standard in audit defence, yet the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie held that written records are not strictly mandatory, as credible oral testimony can fill gaps.

body.text: In Canada's federal SR&ED program, the burden of proof rests on the taxpayer: claimants must adduce evidence that eligible scientific research, including testing, was undertaken. Contemporaneous documentation remains the primary evidentiary standard in audit defence, yet the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie held that written records are not strictly mandatory, as credible oral testimony can fill gaps.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive ecosystem is anchored by the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which oversees technical and financial compliance) and the Department of Finance Canada (which establishes tax policy under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.))1. According to industry advisory figures, the program supports more than 24,160 businesses annually4, with the CRA reporting that small businesses accounted for 65% of all SR&ED claims submitted in the 2025–2026 fiscal year5. The federal SR&ED regime operates through a dual-mechanism architecture: an immediate 100% income tax deduction (or indefinite carryforward) for allowable SR&ED expenditures pooled under Section 37, and a credit-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on qualified SR&ED expenditures under Section 127 and Section 127.11. Between December 2024 and November 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most sweeping legislative modernization in decades8. Enacted into law when Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026—and effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—parliamentary reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds on current expenditures), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average annual revenue phase-out (which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect), reinstated capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024, restored equipment lease costs, and launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322) on April 1, 20261. Furthermore, Federal Budget 2026, tabled on November 5, 2026, proposed a $930 million five-year expansion for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, extending SR&ED eligibility to downstream commercialization testing (regulatory approvals and certifications) and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs10.

At the sub-national level, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits layer onto the federal base, creating combined federal-provincial cash recovery rates that advisory analyses place between 43% and 65% of direct expenditures for qualifying CCPCs15. However, provincial responses to the 2025–2026 federal overhaul have diverged sharply17. British Columbia expressly harmonized its 10% SR&ED tax credit with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out, ECPC refundability, and capital expenditure restoration while making its credit permanent in BC Budget 202617. Quebec executed a structural overhaul for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing four legacy R&D credits and consolidating provincial support into the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital expenditures above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on the excess17. Saskatchewan doubled its 10% CCPC refundable expenditure cap from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 for expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 202417, whereas Ontario (8% refundable OITC on a $3,000,000 cap, 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC, and 20% refundable OBRITC), Alberta (8% base / 20% incremental Innovation Employment Grant on a $4,000,000 cap), Manitoba (15% credit, half refundable for in-house R&D), and the Atlantic Provinces and Yukon (15% fully refundable credits) retained their distinct provincial ceilings and eligibility parameters17.
1. Legislative and Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Historical Evolution and Policy Rationale

Canada first introduced dedicated tax deductions for industrial research and development through 1944 amendments to the Income War Tax Act (the statutory predecessor to the modern Income Tax Act), permitting Canadian corporations to deduct scientific research expenditures against revenue despite general prohibitions on capital deductions under Section 18 of the Act21. The modern structural framework of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program was established in May 1985, when the Department of Finance amended the statutory definition to incorporate the term "experimental development" and clarify that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development are excluded22.

From a public finance perspective, the Department of Finance classifies the SR&ED program as a non-structural tax measure and refundable investment tax credit designed to encourage private-sector R&D performance in Canada and assist small businesses2. Because the economic benefits of scientific and technological advancements spill over beyond the performing enterprise to other businesses and sectors of the economy, private firms operating without government support would perform less SR&ED than is desirable for the overall economy2. Tax credits under the program are classified as deviations from the benchmark tax system because the tax benefit can be obtained in a taxation year other than the year in which it accrues, and the refundable portion is classified as a transfer payment for government accounting purposes2. The SR&ED program delivers non-dilutive tax relief through two distinct yet interconnected statutory mechanisms under the Income Tax Act (ITA)1:

items: The Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool: Allows taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool current and (effective December 16, 2024) qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada and deduct them immediately against business income in the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years6.

The Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC): Allows taxpayers to earn a percentage-based tax credit (ranging from the 15% basic rate to the 35% enhanced rate) on their "qualified expenditures," which can be applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, carried back 3 years, carried forward 20 years, or—for qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, individuals, and certain trusts—paid out directly as a cash refund6.

body.text: 1.3 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: Bill C-15 and Budget 2026
Between late 2024 and late 2026, the Government of Canada enacted and proposed two major waves of SR&ED reform that fundamentally altered the financial modelling of R&D claims in Canada.
Wave 1: The 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025 (Enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026)

In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), released in December 2024, the Department of Finance initially proposed increasing the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs2. Subsequently, Federal Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025) superseded the FES 2024 expenditure limit proposal by further increasing the enhanced expenditure limit from $4,500,000 to $6,000,0002.

All of these measures were introduced in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 (enacted as S.C. 2026, c. 3)1. Crucially, the enacted legislation applies retroactively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (meaning calendar-year corporations qualified starting with their 2025 taxation year beginning January 1, 2025), while the restoration of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs applies to depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (i.e., after December 15, 2024) and lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 20241. In addition, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process using Form T1322, and in May 2026, the CRA released modernized versions of Form T661 (Rev. 26), Schedule T2SCH31, Schedule T2SCH49, Form T1145, and Form T11461.

body.text: Wave 2: Federal Budget 2026 Commercialization and IP Expansion (Tabled November 5, 2026)

On November 5, 2026, the Government of Canada tabled Federal Budget 2026, proposing a second structural expansion of the SR&ED program to bridge the gap between experimental development and commercial deployment10. Applicable to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (subject to legislative enactment, meaning calendar-year corporations will first access these rules in their 2027 taxation year), Budget 2026 (pp. 117, 402–403) allocates $930 million over five years (and $235 million annually thereafter) to bring two previously excluded downstream categories into the SR&ED expenditure base at existing ITC rates (35% enhanced / 15% basic)10:

items: Regulatory Approvals and Product Certifications: Eligible SR&ED activities and expenditures are proposed to expand to cover tests, technological validations, and studies required to satisfy regulatory requirements or obtain initial approvals or certifications necessary to commercialize a new or improved product or process, provided such testing is directly linked to an underlying eligible SR&ED project10. The CRA plans to publish sector-specific administrative guidance delineating qualifying regulatory validation from general commercial marketing10.

Intellectual Property (IP) Registration and Maintenance Costs: Eligible SR&ED expenditures are proposed to expand to include costs reasonably incurred to register, obtain, and maintain statutory protection—under Canadian law or equivalent foreign legislation—for intellectual property developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project13. The covered IP instruments are limited to four statutory categories: patents, certificates of supplementary protection (extending pharmaceutical patent protection), plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software10. Trademarks and industrial designs are excluded14. Supporting technical and legal preparation work (such as preparing and filing patent application materials) must be conducted in Canada to qualify, although official administrative filing and maintenance fees paid directly to foreign IP offices outside Canada are eligible13. Costs incurred to enforce IP rights—such as patent infringement litigation—are excluded13. Furthermore, if a taxpayer subsequently sells or disposes of intellectual property for which SR&ED IP protection deductions and ITCs were claimed, statutory recapture rules will apply to claw back the tax benefit10.

body.text: Notably, although the 2024 Fall Economic Statement had previously signalled consultations toward a preferential "Patent Box" corporate tax rate on IP commercialization income, both Budget 2025 and Budget 2026 omitted any Patent Box tax-rate regime13. Instead, the federal government channelled innovation and capital formation incentives through the expanded SR&ED framework, the $75 million NRC IP Assist Program and $22.5 million Patent Collective (funded in Budget 2025), and the Productivity Mega Deduction (announced September 15, 2026, with draft legislation released October 1, 2026, providing immediate 100% expensing for a broad range of capital assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026, and extended in Budget 2026 to increase the deduction rate for Canadian development expenses from 30% to 100%)10.
2. Technical Eligibility Criteria: Subsection 248(1) and CRA Administrative Guidelines
2.1 The Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1)

Technical eligibility for SR&ED across all industries is governed by a single unified statutory definition in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act8. Under Subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of four qualifying limbs (paragraphs (a) through (d)), while excluding seven prohibited categories (paragraphs (e) through (k))27:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view4. Basic research happens predominantly at universities and research institutes and represents the least common category for corporate claims4.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view15.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto21. The vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada—spanning software engineering, advanced manufacturing, food science, agri-tech, cleantech, and modular construction—are filed under the experimental development limb1.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Eligible Support Work: Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight enumerated categories—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development (paragraphs (a), (b), or (c)) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer1. Support work never qualifies as SR&ED on its own; for example, routine computer programming or engineering design is ineligible unless it is directly supporting and proportionate to an experimental development investigation aimed at resolving a technological uncertainty28.

body.text: 2.2 Mandatory Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Even where a company operates in a scientific or engineering discipline, Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven specific activities from the definition of SR&ED28:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion28.
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes28.
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities (which frequently catches behavioural analytics and consumer data work)28.

Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (if a business conducts SR&ED while prospecting for minerals, the eligible SR&ED work can be claimed while the prospecting work itself must be excluded)28.
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process28.
Paragraph (j): Style changes (such as iterating a product's form, finish, and proportions without resolving an underlying technological uncertainty)28.
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection28.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives emphasize, the critical feature that distinguishes eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as data collection or testing) from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose: if data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of performing scientific research or experimental development, it qualifies as support work under paragraph (d)28.
2.3 The CRA's "Why" and "How" Framework vs. The Five Questions

Historically, following Information Circular IC 86-4R3 (1994) and the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998), the CRA evaluated technical eligibility using a Five-Question Framework set out in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (first published in 2012, revised in 2015, and archived in 2021)22:

items: Was there a scientific or technological uncertainty?1
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?1
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?1
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement?1
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?1

body.text: On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced the archived policy paper with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, restructuring the analytical presentation into two mandatory statutory requirements: the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement22. As confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), this two-part framework did not alter the substantive law of Northwest Hydraulic; rather, it maps the five common law questions directly onto the two clauses of Subsection 248(1)22.
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement)

The "Why" requirement asks why the work was conducted: it must be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement1. A technological advancement can only be sought where the project confronts a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty—defined as a limitation, gap, or constraint in publicly available scientific or technological knowledge and standard engineering practice such that a competent professional in the field cannot determine in advance whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it1. Overcoming business problems, configuring cloud services by following vendor documentation, or acquiring existing know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not satisfy the "Why" requirement28.

Crucially, technological uncertainty often arises at the system level when integrating known components or technologies whose combined interactions create unpredictable conflicts—such as latency bottlenecks, state synchronization failures, or power stability constraints—that cannot be resolved through standard engineering procedures58. Moreover, a project does not need to succeed commercially or achieve its target performance to qualify1. The advancement lies in the generation of new scientific or technological knowledge—including establishing through systematic experimentation that an approach does not work1.
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

The "How" requirement captures Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic, asking how the work was conducted: it must be carried out by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis1. Under the CRA guidelines, a systematic investigation requires four sequential elements22:

items: Formulation of a Hypothesis: Generating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving an objective or resolving a problem (expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach)22.
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Subjecting the idea or hypothesis to testing by means of experiment or analysis (where the idea can evolve and change as a result of testing)22.
Development of Logical Conclusions: Developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis21.

Contemporaneous Evidence Keeping: Keeping evidence generated as the work progresses—such as dated trial logs, test results, revised shop drawings, prototype photos, Git commit logs, and issue trackers—that substantiates the hypotheses tested and conclusions reached4.

body.text: 3. Federal Financial Mechanics: Rates, Caps, Phase-Outs, and Refundability
3.1 The Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool

Before computing the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit, a claimant must compute its Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Subsection 37(1) on Part 3 of Form T6611. An amount can be deductible under Section 37 without generating an ITC in the same amount: for example, 100% of an arm's length SR&ED contract enters the Section 37 pool, whereas only 80% enters the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool; conversely, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount enters the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool but never enters the Section 37 pool1.
Under Subsection 37(1), the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is increased by specific statutory additions and decreased by specific statutory reductions7:

items: Pool Additions: Paragraph 37(1)(a) adds current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer (subparas. 37(1)(a)(i) and (i.01)), plus third-party payments to Canadian resident corporations (subpara. 37(1)(a)(i.1)) and approved entities (subparas. 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii))7. Paragraph 37(1)(b)—restored by Bill C-15 for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024—adds expenditures of a capital nature made on depreciable property (other than buildings or leasehold interests in buildings, except special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903) intended for all or substantially all (≥90%) SR&ED use or value consumption in Canada6. Under Subsection 37(6), any amount deducted under Subsection 37(1) in respect of capital expenditures is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer, precluding duplicate depreciation on Schedule T2SCH85. Further additions include repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (para. 37(1)(c)), amounts previously included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(v) (para. 37(1)(c.1)), and prior-year SR&ED ITC recapture amounts and partnership ITC recapture excess amounts (paras. 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3))7.

Pool Reductions and Loss Restriction Events: Paragraph 37(1)(d) reduces the pool by government assistance and non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received7. Paragraph 37(1)(d.1) deducts provincial super-allowance benefit amounts7. Paragraph 37(1)(e) reduces the pool by SR&ED ITCs claimed against Part I tax or refunded in the preceding taxation year7. (If the pool balance becomes negative—or as noted under Paragraph 12(1)(t) / Paragraph 12(1)(v) when prior-year ITCs exceed the pool—the negative amount is included in taxable income in the following year)7. Paragraphs 37(1)(f) and (f.1) deduct amounts claimed under Subsection 37(1) or insolvency Section 61.3 in preceding taxation years7. Finally, under Paragraph 37(1)(h) and Subsection 37(6.1), upon a Loss Restriction Event (an acquisition of control of a corporation or a new majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), there is a deemed year-end and the Section 37 pool is reduced to nil; the undeducted pre-acquisition balance can only be reinstated and deducted in subsequent taxation years if the business to which the expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit (or with a reasonable expectation of profit), and only to the extent of income derived from that same business or a similar business6.

body.text: Any portion of an earned SR&ED ITC that is not refunded in cash or applied against current-year Part I tax may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset Part I tax otherwise payable12. Under Subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded to a taxpayer in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax, thereby reducing the remaining ITC pool available for carryforward or carryback12. Just like the Section 37 pool, unused ITC carryforwards and post-acquisition ITC carrybacks are subject to "same or similar business" streaming restrictions upon an acquisition of control12.
3.3 Expenditure Limit Formulas: CCPCs, Associated Groups, and ECPCs

Under Subsection 127(10.1), a qualifying CCPC or (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) earns an additional 20% ITC (bringing the total ITC rate to 35%) on qualified expenditures up to its annual Expenditure Limit6. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for prior taxation years)9.
1. The CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

Unless a CCPC elects to use the revenue method, its $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is phased out based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and any associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year6. Under Bill C-15, the phase-out begins at $15,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and reaches nil at $75,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000)9. Expressed as a formula:
CCPC Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000]

In this formula, A is $0 if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined across the associated group) is ≤$15,000,000, and otherwise A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,00012. Every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit by $100,00048: at $15,000,000 taxable capital, the Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000 (maximum 35% credit of $2,100,000); at $35,000,000 taxable capital (A = $20,000,000), the limit is $4,000,000 (maximum 35% credit of $1,400,000); at $45,000,000 taxable capital (A = $30,000,000), the limit is $3,000,000 (maximum 35% credit of $1,050,000); at $60,000,000 taxable capital (A = $45,000,000), the limit is $1,500,000 (maximum 35% credit of $525,000); and at ≥$75,000,000 taxable capital (A = $60,000,000), the limit reaches $08.

Prior-year taxable income does not reduce the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit itself, but determines whether a CCPC meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under Subsection 127.1(2)12. Specifically, under Subsection 127.1(2.01), a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation still receives 100% refundability on its 35% ITC for current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures) within its $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit6. Status as a "qualifying corporation"—which requires that the prior-year taxable income of the CCPC and its associated corporations not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit—matters for earning 40% cash refundability on the 15% basic ITC above the Expenditure Limit12. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit is calculated as:
Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000]

where A is nil when prior-year taxable capital is ≤$15,000,000, and otherwise the excess over $15,000,000 (capped at $60,000,000, so the Qualifying Income Limit hits zero at $75,000,000 of taxable capital)12.
2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the Revenue Election (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), & 127(10.32))

Under Bill C-15, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) (Subsection 127(9)) can access the 35% enhanced refundable ITC up to the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit6. Under Subsection 127(10.6), an ECPC's $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is phased out using the average annual revenue reflected in its financial statements (or consolidated group financial statements) over the three preceding fiscal years, starting at $15,000,000 and becoming nil at $75,000,0006:
ECPC Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − R) ÷ $60,000,000]

where R is nil if three-year average annual revenue is ≤$15,000,000, and otherwise the excess of three-year average annual revenue over $15,000,000 (up to $60,000,000)12. Under Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a standalone CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs (provided all CCPCs in the group jointly elect) may opt out of the 127(10.2) taxable capital test and elect to compute their Expenditure Limit under Subsection 127(10.6) using the three-year average annual revenue test6.
3. Associated CCPCs, Consolidated ECPCs, and Short Taxation Years

Associated CCPCs (Subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.4)) must share a single $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit)5. Paralleling the associated CCPC rules, under Subsections 127(10.61), 127(10.62), and 127(10.63), an ECPC that is a member of a "consolidated group" (Subsection 127(9)) has a default Expenditure Limit of nil unless the group files an election allocating the group's 127(10.6) Expenditure Limit among its ECPC members6. If an associated CCPC group or consolidated ECPC group fails to file the allocation agreement within 30 days of a request by the Minister, the Minister allocates the limit (Subsections 127(10.4) and 127(10.63))6. Under Subsections 127(10.5) and 127(10.64), if a CCPC or ECPC has a short taxation year of less than 51 weeks, its Expenditure Limit must be prorated by multiplying the limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365; similarly, any short fiscal year in the three-year revenue lookback period must have its financial statement revenue grossed up by multiplying by 365 and dividing by the number of days in that short fiscal year6.

body.text: Deep Dive: The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Overall Cap (Regulations 2900(4) & 2900(6))

Under Regulation 2900(4), the Prescribed Proxy Amount is fixed at 55% of the salary base (reduced from 65% for 2012 and prior years and 60% for 2013)34. The salary base (Part 5 of Form T661) comprises the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible foreign SR&ED salaries under Subsection 37(1.5)), excluding for all employees (Regulation 2900(9)): taxable benefits under Section 6, stock option benefits under Section 7, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310), and employer-paid related benefits32.

To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures made in the year, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA using the formula A − B − C34:

items: A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold)34.

B is the total of all deductions claimed in the year under specific provisions of the Income Tax Act: Section 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance, interest expense, bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (deductible SR&ED expenditures, per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts)34.
C is the total of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent)34.

body.text: As the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy notes, this overall cap generally does not restrict the PPA if the claimant deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED business expenses (excluding the specified B and C deductions) for each $100 of eligible salary in the salary base34.
Deep Dive: Traditional Method "Directly Related" and "Incremental" Tests (Regulations 2900(2)(c) & 2900(3))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, claimants electing the Traditional Method can only claim overhead expenditures on Line 360 if the expenditure satisfies both the Directly Related Test and the Incremental Test33:

items: Directly Related Test: There must be a direct linkage—proceeding without deviation, interruption, intervening step, or intermediary—between the expenditure and (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED30. For example, while the wages of a human resources, accounting, or purchasing clerk who performs non-technological duties aiding ongoing SR&ED can qualify on Line 360 if incremental, the employer's share of related benefits, training costs, retiring allowances, or travel costs for that clerical employee are never allowed because the CRA views them as "overhead on overhead" separated by an intermediate step26. Similarly, headhunter fees, recruitment advertising, candidate interview travel, and immigration/work permit/visa fees are disqualified as general business expenses, whereas moving expenses to relocate selected candidates or SR&ED employees to another facility within Canada qualify26. Furthermore, fees paid for preparing SR&ED claims (both accounting and technical portions), costs to attend technical conventions or conferences, and interest on borrowed money are prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 and cannot earn an ITC (though internal employee salaries for preparing SR&ED claims are not prescribed expenditures if directly related and incremental)33.

Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred33. Variable utilities (such as electricity, gas, or water allocated by equipment usage time) meet the incremental test, whereas a fixed-cost equipment maintenance contract or recurring fixed monthly telephone, cellular, or internet access charge fails the incremental test because the cost does not vary with SR&ED usage33. Waste disposal costs incurred after the SR&ED activity that produced the scrap has finished also fail the incremental test33.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and Foreign Work

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), allowable salaries and wages must be incurred in the taxation year and paid within the taxation year or within 180 days after the end of the taxation year (Subsection 78(4))25. Any salary or wage unpaid 180 days after fiscal year-end must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 (excluded from the current year's deduction and ITC) and can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid25.

Whether an employee is "directly engaged in SR&ED" is a question of fact based on the tasks performed rather than the employee's job title27. Eligible tasks include hands-on experimentation and analysis, the eight paragraph 248(1)(d) support categories, operating an experimental machine or feeding raw materials under technical supervision, direct technical supervision of SR&ED staff, technological feasibility studies, technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects, and preparing internal technical documentation31. Under Regulation 2900(5), if an employee spends all or substantially all (≥90%) of their working time on SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary qualifies26.

Special statutory restrictions apply to "specified employees" (Subsections 248(1), 37(9), 37(9.1), and Regulation 2900(7))—defined as any employee who is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year (together with non-arm's length persons such as spouses, siblings, or controlled corporations), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer30:

items: Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): All bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are disallowed for both the Section 37 pool and the Section 127 ITC (unless the employee's only remuneration for performing SR&ED duties consists of bonuses or profit-based pay, in which case an amount commensurate with those duties may be allowed under CRA administrative policy)1. Dividends do not constitute salary or wages and never qualify1.

5 × YMPE Cap on Direct SR&ED Salary (Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a specified employee in the Section 37 pool and for direct ITC calculation is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the tax year30. For the 2026 calendar year, the YMPE is $74,600, yielding a maximum specified employee SR&ED salary cap of $373,000 (5 × $74,600)35. If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the $373,000 cap must be allocated among the associated group using Form T1174 (Subsections 37(9.2)–(9.5))30.

75% / 2.5 × YMPE Cap on the Proxy Salary Base (Regulations 2900(7) & 2900(8)): When computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method, the amount included for a specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year), or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (2.5 × YMPE × [Days Employed ÷ 365])34. For the 2026 calendar year (YMPE = $74,600), the maximum proxy salary base per specified employee is $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600), which must also be shared across associated corporations34.

body.text: Finally, under Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), while foreign contractor payments and foreign overhead costs never qualify for ITCs, a claimant can claim "permissible salary or wages" on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661 for SR&ED performed outside Canada up to a maximum limit of 10% of the total SR&ED salary and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada7. All five statutory conditions must be satisfied: (1) the work was done directly by an employee (not a contractor), (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred, (3) the work was related to the business of the claimant, (4) the work done outside Canada was an integral part of and solely in support of the SR&ED project carried out in Canada, and (5) the salary or wages paid are not subject to income or profits tax from another country30.
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method) and Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method), claimants can deduct and earn ITCs on the laid-down or manufactured cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada26. Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, an item constitutes "materials for SR&ED" only if it is a physical, tangible substance (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process composes the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being performed, or that results from the SR&ED26. Items that do not compose the body of the experimental object—such as broken or used laboratory supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, or general utilities—do not qualify as materials and can only be claimed as overhead under the Traditional Method26. However, process water (which chemically enters an intermediate or final product and is rendered valueless as process feed) and energy used directly in endothermic reactions (in chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, metallurgical, cement, glass, or ceramics processes where energy is retained in the physical form of the product) qualify as materials consumed26.

The policy distinguishes sharply between materials consumed—materials that are destroyed, absorbed, broken down, or rendered virtually valueless (sold or valued at 10% or less of original cost) as a result of SR&ED, which never trigger recapture—and materials transformed, which are changed in shape, structure, or function or incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production run while retaining a value greater than 10% of their original cost26. If transformed materials are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the claimant is subject to ITC Recapture under Subsection 127(27)46.
4.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's length party (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and Subsection 127(9)) to perform SR&ED (or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work) on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, while 80% of the expenditure is included in qualified expenditures to earn the Section 127 ITC25. To earn an ITC, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" and the SR&ED work must physically take place in Canada33. Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, in an SR&ED contract, the payer controls the work, rights to the work are exclusive to the payer, and the tax treatment is on an accrual basis31. For expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 repealed the former "capital look-through rule" in Subsections 37(14) and 37(15)6.

Conversely, when a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (Subsections 127(9), 127(11.6), and 127(13)), the contract payment is deductible by the payer under Section 37, but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures (Paragraph 127(9)(f)) and earns $0 in ITCs directly31. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own SR&ED expenditures (without reducing them by the contract payment received) and may transfer all or part of its qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the NAL payer by jointly filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length)44. Partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 because a partnership is not considered a "person" under Subsection 127(13)39. Furthermore, if a claimant purchases goods, non-SR&ED services, materials, or capital property from a NAL supplier, Subsection 127(11.6) caps the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes at the actual cost (or capital cost) incurred by the NAL supplier, eliminating any intercompany profit element6.

Finally, Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii)), governed by the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy and reported on Form T1263, are payments made to eligible research entities where the performer controls the SR&ED, multiple funders typically participate, and the claimant obtains a non-exclusive/preferential right to exploit the results in its business31. Like arm's length contracts, third-party payments are 100% deductible under Section 37 and 80% eligible for ITC under Section 12725. Eligible recipients comprise six statutory categories: A Entities (37(1)(a)(i.1), Canadian resident corporations, where incentives are earned in the year the SR&ED is performed), B Entities (37(1)(a)(ii), approved associations), C Entities (37(1)(a)(ii), approved universities, colleges, and research institutes), D Entities (37(1)(a)(ii), non-profit SR&ED corporations exempt under Paragraph 149(1)(j)), E Entities (37(1)(a)(ii), approved granting councils), and F Entities (37(1)(a)(iii), 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations for basic or applied research in Canada)31.
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Cloud Computing

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA published three updated administrative policies in May and June 2026 governing capital and leased assets acquired after December 15, 20245:

items: All or Substantially All (ASA) Capital Property (SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, updated June 29, 2026): Under Paragraph 37(1)(b) and Subsection 127(9), a claimant can claim 100% of the capital cost of new depreciable property acquired and available for use (Subsection 127(11.2)) after December 15, 2024, if at the time of acquisition the claimant intends either that the property will be used all or substantially all (≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or that ≥90% of its value will be consumed in SR&ED in Canada5. While used depreciable property can be deducted in the Section 37 pool (Line 390), used or regularly demonstrated property is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 and cannot earn an ITC (unless a lessor acquires brand-new unleased property and jointly elects with the first lessee to deem direct acquisition)5. Land (non-depreciable), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under Paragraph 37(8)(e), except for a prescribed special-purpose building under Section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations (amended by Section 109 of S.C. 2026, c. 3), which requires working areas engineered to have a displacement in any direction of not more than 0.02 µm (micrometres) and an interior airspace containing, per 0.028 cubic metre, not more than: (a) 350 airborne particles ≤0.1 µm (and zero >0.1 µm), (b) 75 particles ≤0.2 µm (and zero >0.2 µm), (c) 30 particles ≤0.3 µm (and zero >0.3 µm), or (d) 10 particles ≤0.5 µm (and zero >0.5 µm)6. On Form T661 (Rev. 26), claimants list the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties per project on Line 262 and report the 20 most expensive capital properties across the claim in Part 6B (Boxes 780, 782, and 786)5.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, updated May 22, 2026): When new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, does not meet the 90% ASA threshold because it is shared between SR&ED and commercial work, it may qualify for ITCs (reported on Line 504 and Part 6C, Boxes 788, 790, and 792 of Form T661) as First-Term SUE and Second-Term SUE (Subsections 127(9) and 127(11.5)(b))5. To qualify, the property must be brand-new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, must not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (equipment intended at acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial plant/facility and intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life)45. First-Term SUE is evaluated at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after the equipment was acquired and available for use (First Period); if actual SR&ED operating time during the First Period is primarily (>50%) of total operating time, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowing costs under Section 21 and adjusted for NAL rules under 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC6. Second-Term SUE is evaluated at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition (Second Period); if actual SR&ED operating time from acquisition through the end of the Second Period remains >50%, a second 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (up to 50% of capital cost across both periods)5. SUE capital cost never enters the Section 37 pool; it is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8 under normal CCA rules, and any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year5.

Equipment Lease Costs (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, updated June 8, 2026): Lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are claimable on Lines 350 and 355 of Form T661, with operating time measured across the full 12-month taxation year (or the post-December 15, 2024 period in a straddle year)5. Under the Proxy Method, equipment used ASA (≥90%) is 100% claimable, equipment used primarily (>50% to <90%) is 50% claimable, and equipment used ≤50% is 0% claimable; GPOEF (desks, chairs, photocopiers, telephones) and building rent are excluded, though computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are explicitly not considered GPOEF and therefore qualify31. Under the Traditional Method, equipment (including GPOEF) leased and used ASA (≥90%) is 100% claimable as a lease expenditure, while equipment used <90% is claimable as overhead on Line 360 proportional to actual SR&ED operating time if directly related and incremental5.

Cloud Computing, GPUs, and Software Infrastructure: For software, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) claimants, the post-December 15, 2024 restoration of capital and lease expenditures makes dedicated on-premise GPU clusters and compute infrastructure acquired or leased after December 15, 2024, claimable directly as ASA capital property, SUE, or leased equipment4. Conversely, elastic cloud computing costs are treated as overhead expenditures: they are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method and can only be claimed separately on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if the claimant maintains segregated cloud cost accounts for "development/R&D infrastructure" versus "production infrastructure" to prove the costs are directly related and incremental33.

body.text: 4.6 Investment Tax Credit Recapture (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and Subsections 127(27) through 127(36), previously earned SR&ED ITCs are recaptured—and added directly to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable—when four conditions are met47: (1) the taxpayer acquired a particular property (materials transformed, ASA capital property, Shared-Use Equipment, or physical property resulting from an SR&ED contract) in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (Subsection 127(36)), (2) the cost of the property was included as a qualified expenditure, (3) an ITC was earned on that expenditure, and (4) in the current year, the taxpayer disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use (or disposes of/converts another product or asset that incorporates the property)47.

The recapture addition to Part I tax equals the lesser of the actual ITC earned on the property or the applicable ITC rate (e.g., 35% or 15%) multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property at the time of commercial conversion or non-arm's length disposition45. Crucially, recapture applies only to the physical material or capital property acquisition cost (Subsection 127(32)) and never applies to in-house SR&ED salaries, wages, or overhead47. Furthermore, the CRA administratively waives recapture under a 10% de minimis rule if scrap sale proceeds or FMV upon conversion are less than 10% of the original cost of the property46, and any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax is restored to increase the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year (Paragraph 37(1)(c.2))7.

Nearly every Canadian province (and the Yukon Territory) administers a statutory R&D tax credit that piggybacks on the federal Subsection 248(1) technical definition of SR&ED15. 1. Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario operates a three-tier corporate R&D tax credit system under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered by the CRA19:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule T2SCH566): Provides an 8% refundable tax credit (entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5) to qualifying corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations)17. As of October 2026, Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit; the OITC remains capped at $3,000,000, its expenditure base is described in CRA guidance as covering 100% of current expenditures (without confirmation that restored federal capital expenditures have been added to the OITC base), and its $3,000,000 limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income rises from $500,000 to $800,000 or when prior-year specified capital rises from $25,000,000 to $50,000,00017.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45, Schedule T2SCH508): Provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (entered on Line 416 of Schedule 5; rate reduced from 4.5% on June 1, 2016) to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure limit19. Unused ORDTC balances can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, and recapture applies under Section 45 (entered on Line 277 of Schedule 5)19. Because provincial R&D credits constitute "government assistance" under federal Subsection 127(11.1) and Paragraph 37(1)(d)—reducing the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base in the year earned—Ontario law permits corporations to formally waive all or part of the ORDTC (Subsection 43(1)) or OITC (Subsection 96(14)) with their T2 return (on or before 6 months after year-end or on an amended return) so that an unusable non-refundable ORDTC does not reduce their 35% federal cash refund19.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules T2SCH568 & T2SCH569): Provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible research contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs) in Ontario, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap shared across an associated group19.

body.text: 2. Quebec: The 2025–2026 Consolidation into the CRIC

In its 2025–2026 Budget Plan (March 2025), the Government of Quebec enacted a sweeping restructuring of provincial innovation tax assistance17. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished four separate legacy credits—(1) the R&D Wages Tax Credit, (2) the University / Public Research Centre Tax Credit, (3) the Pre-Competitive Private Partnership Research Tax Credit, and (4) the Research Consortium Fees and Dues Tax Credit—and consolidated them into a single measure: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), governed by Sections 1029.8 et seq. of the Quebec Taxation Act and administered by Revenu Québec18.

While Quebec harmonizes its core R&D definition with the federal SR&ED definition (relying on the CRA for scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands provincial eligibility to cover pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec as a continuation of Quebec R&D work, including: testing, prototyping, and technological validation; studies and validations required to obtain initial regulatory approvals or certifications; product design involving form, aesthetics, functionality, or material selection; and specific quality control activities required for initial approvals or certifications17. Eligible CRIC expenditures cover wages paid to employees engaged in eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities (including direct support roles), 50% of arm's length Quebec subcontractor payments (requiring the subcontractor's QST number or SIN), payments to eligible research organizations, and new depreciable capital property used in Quebec almost exclusively in eligible activities (excluding land, buildings, and rights in buildings)17.

Before any CRIC is earned, net eligible expenditures must exceed an Exclusion Threshold, defined as the greater of $50,000 (prorated for the number of days in the taxation year) or an amount calculated using the basic personal amount applicable to the involved employees18. Once the Exclusion Threshold is exceeded, the CRIC is 100% refundable at 30% on the first $1,000,000 of net eligible expenditures (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN, though partnership members are limited to the 20% base rate) and 20% on all excess net eligible expenditures18. Claimants must file Form RD-222 (for the deduction of R&D expenditures) and Form RD-1029.8.CR (to compute the CRIC, reported on the CO-17 return under Code 112 for R&D and Code 113 for pre-commercialization) within 12 months of the CO-17 filing deadline18.
3. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

items: British Columbia (Form T666): Under Sections 97–103 of the Income Tax Act (BC), qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn a 10% refundable tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified BC expenditures (including restored capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024), phased out over $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital17. Expenditures above the limit, and expenditures by other corporations, earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years), and BC Budget 2026 made the BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent17.

Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (AT1 Schedule 29): Governed by Sections 26.95–26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020), the IEG provides a two-tier 100% refundable grant/credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (maximum annual payout of $800,000; filing deadline 15 months after the filing due date, i.e., 21 months after year-end, though practitioners advise aligning with the 18-month federal SR&ED window)17. Layer 1 provides an 8% refundable benefit on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's "base level of spending" (its average eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years), while Layer 2 provides an additional 12% incremental benefit—for a combined 20% refundable rate—on eligible spending exceeding that two-year baseline17. For example, if an Alberta corporation spent $1,200,000 in Year T-2 and $1,800,000 in Year T-1, its two-year baseline is ($1,200,000 + $1,800,000) ÷ 2 = $1,500,000; if it spends $3,000,000 in Year T, the first $1,500,000 earns 8% ($120,000) and the next $1,500,000 earns 20% ($300,000), yielding $420,00072.

Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403), Manitoba (Schedule T2SCH380), Atlantic Provinces (T2SCH340, T2SCH360, T2SCH301), and Yukon (T2SCH442): Saskatchewan provides a 10% refundable credit for CCPCs on their first $2,000,000 of annual qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024 (doubled from $1,000,000), and a 10% non-refundable credit above $2,000,000 and for non-CCPCs, capped at $1,000,000 in combined annual credits17. Manitoba provides a 15% credit (including current and non-building capital expenditures) that is 100% refundable when conducted under contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute, and 50% refundable (7.5%) / 50% non-refundable (7.5%) for in-house R&D15. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon all provide a 15% fully refundable credit (with Yukon adding a 5% bonus for amounts paid or payable to Yukon University, and Newfoundland and Labrador uniquely not reducing provincial eligible expenditures for government or non-government assistance other than GST/HST input tax credits)15.

body.text: 6. Direct Innovation Grants and Federal-Provincial Stacking Mechanics
6.1 Statutory Treatment of Assistance and Contract Payments (ITA 37(1)(d), 127(11.1), & 127(18))

Under Canadian tax law, direct innovation grants, wage subsidies, forgivable loans, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits coexist with the federal SR&ED program, but the Income Tax Act prohibits claiming the same dollar twice16. Governed by the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026)42:

items: Government and Non-Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9), 127(11.1), & Paragraph 12(1)(x)): Government assistance includes any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), or investment allowance from a government, municipality, or public authority, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself, clean economy ITCs under Subsections 127.44 to 127.491, and an "excluded loan" as defined in Subsection 12(11)5. Non-government assistance includes any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance included under Paragraph 12(1)(x)32.

Contract Payments (Subsection 127(9) & Subsection 127(18)): Any amount paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's length taxable supplier, or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity (Section 149), for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf reduces the performer's qualified expenditures on a project-by-project basis38. Under Subsection 127(19) and the CRA policy, if assistance or contract payments for a specific project exceed total project costs in the current year, the excess carries forward to reduce qualified expenditures on that project in subsequent years (and if an agreement fails to separate payments for eligible vs. non-eligible work, the entire payment reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures)42. Non-arm's length groups may allocate assistance among group members using Form T114542.

Sequential Stacking Order and Proxy Overhead Preservation: When stacking grants, provincial tax credits, and federal SR&ED on Part 4 of Form T661, direct grants (such as NRC IRAP) are deducted first16. Crucially, when an NRC IRAP grant reimburses employee SR&ED wages, those reimbursed wage dollars are removed from the net qualified expenditure pool, but the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead associated with those employees remains fully claimable for SR&ED16. Second, provincial R&D tax credits are calculated16. Third, the provincial R&D tax credit is subtracted as government assistance from the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool, and the 35% (or 15%) federal SR&ED ITC is computed on the remaining balance16. Under the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit relating to the notional 55% PPA reduces federal qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, but is not deducted from the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (instead, it is included in income on Schedule T2SCH1 in the year received)26.

body.text: 6.2 Major Federal Direct R&D Funding Programs (2026)

items: National Research Council of Canada — Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP): Established in 1962, NRC IRAP provides technical advisory services and non-repayable R&D contributions to incorporated, for-profit Canadian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs; sole proprietorships, partnerships, cooperatives, ULCs, and LLCs are ineligible)16. According to program data, IRAP covers up to 80% of eligible costs (reimbursing monthly claims within 35 business days), with an advertised maximum of up to $10,000,000, a typical award range of $75,000 to $1,000,000, and a median award of $75,000 (overall average $94,000; per-firm average $168,000 across 2,518 businesses funded in 2025)16. IRAP only funds work performed from the date of the signed contribution agreement onward following evaluation by a Client Engagement Advisor (CEA) and an Industrial Technology Advisor (ITA)16. Alongside core R&D project funding and the Youth Employment Program, specialized 2025–2026 IRAP streams include IP Assist ($75 million allocated in Budget 2025), AI Assist (supporting generative AI and deep learning integration), IRAP Clean Technology (renewed with $298 million in Budget 2026), and the Defence Industry Assist (DI Assist) stream (launched in January 2026 with $240 million+ over multiple years for SMEs developing dual-use and defence technologies)10.

Strategic Response Fund (SRF — Formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund [SIF]): Administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), Canada's flagship large-scale industrial R&D and capital investment program—formerly known as the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF)—was rebranded in 2025–2026 as the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)83. Operating on continuous intake with mandatory pre-consultation, the SRF provides large-scale repayable and non-repayable contributions (with announced 2025–2026 SRF project awards ranging from $8,000,000 to $240,000,000 on total project costs of $42,000,000 to $725,000,000) focused on trade resilience, tariff response, domestic AI compute capacity, semiconductors, biomanufacturing, aerospace, clean technology, and supply-chain strengthening in steel, aluminum, automotive, and forestry84. Federal Budget 2026 announced a $1 billion recapitalization over six years for the Strategic Response Fund starting in the 2028–2029 fiscal year10.

body.text: 7. Governance, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence
7.1 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Zero-Discretion Bar (Subsections 37(11) & 220(2.2))

Under Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file Form T661 and the applicable investment tax credit schedule (Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts) containing all prescribed information on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year32:

items: Corporations: Because a T2 Corporation Income Tax Return is due 6 months after fiscal year-end (Paragraph 150(1)(a)), the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year32.

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships): Because an individual carrying on a business has a T1 filing due date of June 15 of the following calendar year, the SR&ED reporting deadline is June 15 of the subsequent year (17.5 months after the December 31 taxation year-end)36.
Trusts: Because a T3 Trust Income Tax and Information Return is due 90 days after the trust's year-end, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 15 months after the trust's taxation year-end36.

Partnerships: Under the CRA's Filing Requirements Policy and SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool (it must deduct 100% of the pool in computing partnership net income in the year incurred) and allocates a 15% ITC to active partners (Subsection 127(8), excluding "specified members" such as limited partners or passive partners)36. If the partnership is required to file a T5013 Partnership Information Return, the partnership's Form T661 should be filed no later than the earliest partner's SR&ED reporting deadline; if exempt from T5013, each partner must file the partnership's Form T661 and their own T2SCH31 / T2038(IND) by their respective deadline36.

body.text: Pursuant to Subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, the CRA is statutorily prohibited from exercising ministerial discretion under Subsection 220(2.1) to waive or extend the SR&ED reporting deadline37. If a corporation files Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 after the 18-month deadline (unless the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, in which case it is extended to the next business day), the entire SR&ED claim is permanently statute-barred4. If Form T661 is filed on time before the 18-month deadline but Schedule T2SCH31 is filed late, the allowable expenditures may still be included in the Section 37 deductible pool, but the corporation cannot earn any Section 127 ITC36.

body.text: 7.3 CRA Review Mechanics, Service Standards, and the Four-Step Escalation Process

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026, replacing The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants)5, the CRA processes claims against established service standards:

items: Refundable SR&ED Claims: 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (which the CRA targets meeting 90% of the time)90.

Pre-Claim Approved Claims (Expenditure-Only Review): 90 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (provided the executed work did not differ significantly from the T1322 approval and no unapproved projects were included)90.
Non-Refundable SR&ED Claims: No established service standard in current CRA guidance90.

body.text: Once the CRA selects a claim for review (via risk assessment or random sampling), the claimant cannot withdraw the SR&ED claim; Part 10 certification is an irrevocable part of the income tax return, and providing incomplete or inaccurate information can result in monetary penalties (Subsection 163(2))1. Reviews are conducted jointly (primarily via virtual videoconferencing, or on-site on an exceptional basis) by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates technical eligibility under Subsection 248(1) and issues an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who examines expenditure allowability and issues a Proposal Letter offering a 30-day window for written representations)37.
If disagreements arise during a review, the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns establish a formal Four-Step Escalation Process37:

items: Step 1 — Talk to the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR): Openly discussing eligibility and financial issues and submitting additional supporting documentation or written representations within the 30-day proposal response window37.
Step 2 — Contact the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM): Elevating unresolved concerns to the reviewers' immediate managers to review the facts of the case37.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the Proposal Package and before the file is closed (before the 30-day proposal period expires), the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre37. Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review determines whether the claimant was given procedural due process and whether the RTA/FR reviews were consistent with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, resulting in either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered37.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection (Form RC592) and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Within 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection (Form RC592) (or online via My Business Account / Represent a Client) with the CRA Appeals Branch37. (Note that a "large corporation" whose total taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000 must reasonably describe each issue, specify the exact dollar relief sought, and pay 50% of the disputed amount upfront)37. If the dispute remains unresolved following the Appeals Officer's review, the taxpayer can appeal to the Tax Court of Canada37.

body.text: 8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

Because terms such as "technological uncertainty", "technological advancement", and "routine engineering" are not defined in the Income Tax Act, Canadian SR&ED law is governed by binding jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA)22.

headers: Judicial Holding & Precedential Impact on SR&ED Audits

cells: Established that SR&ED requires a systematic investigation or search where solutions are systematically tested, distinguishing eligible R&D from ad-hoc trial-and-error shop-floor troubleshooting92.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839)22
Hydraulic physical scale modelling (4 of 5 projects won)66.

Foundational Precedent: Chief Justice Bowman established the Five-Question Test, defined "routine engineering" as techniques/procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, recognized "system uncertainty", and confirmed that failed trials constitute technological advancement22.
Construction moisture-barrier device (Taxpayer won on appeal)66.

Held that while the taxpayer bears the burden of adducing evidence that scientific research (including testing) was undertaken, written documentation is not strictly mandatory in every circumstance; credible oral testimony can bridge gaps in written records21.

Formally adopted the Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Test at the Federal Court of Appeal and held that evaluating, testing, and configuring complex commercial hardware/software reflects the work of "competent and prudent users" rather than computer science SR&ED21.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77)58

Held that ongoing system-level technological uncertainties (resolving paper curling and balancing static vs. dynamic motor power consumption to prevent stalling within a 1.5" × 1.5" × 10" form factor) remained eligible experimental development in subsequent years58.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6)60

Justice Sommerfeldt defined a "hypothesis" as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" and ruled against the taxpayer because no qualified mechanical engineers testified to prove the work exceeded routine engineering21.
Cited as a key Tax Court precedent on experimental development eligibility for manufacturing and process trials1.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) & National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2020 TCC 47; aff'd 2022 FCA 72)22
Metal stamping (Kam-Press) & dynamic SQL database software (National R&D) (Taxpayers lost)22.

The FCA reaffirmed that Northwest Hydraulic is the binding legal interpretation of Subsection 248(1), holding that the CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" guidelines are not binding on courts and still command "an underlying rigour or discipline in the experimental process"22.
Logic Data Products Inc. (2021 TCC), Dave's Diesel Inc. (2022 TCC), JEC Distributors Inc. (2022 TCC), & Paveit Construction Inc. (2025 TCC)60
Electronics, diesel injectors, and construction equipment (Taxpayers lost)60.

Established that technological uncertainty is strictly an objective test measured against the knowledge of competent professionals in the field—not the subjective lack of knowledge of the claimant—and underscored the critical importance of independent expert witness testimony60.
Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC) & Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC)21
Food manufacturing / recipe & canning development (Taxpayers won)21.

Applying Northwest Hydraulic, Joel Theatrical Rigging, and RIS-Christie, the TCC held that structured food-science trials (testing salt/fat reduction, freeze-thaw structural integrity, and preservative-free shelf life) where failed recipes were systematically analysed and modified constituted valid SR&ED, and credible CEO oral testimony filled documentation gaps21.

Recognized systemic uncertainty in open-source tool integration (React/Redux) beyond routine debugging; noted at para. 119 that while contemporaneous timesheets are preferred, they are not strictly required if metrics and reliable testimony substantiate the work (though claims relying on substantially reconstructed post-hoc documentation face denial)65.

body.text: Synthesis of Judicial Principles for Audit Defence
Three overarching doctrinal rules emerge from recent Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence through late 2026:

items: The Objective "Competent Professional" Standard (Northwest Hydraulic, JEC Distributors, Paveit Construction): A taxpayer cannot establish technological uncertainty merely by showing that a product did not previously exist or that the taxpayer's own staff did not know how to build it60. The uncertainty must represent an objective gap in publicly accessible scientific or engineering knowledge across the relevant professional community21. In litigation before the Tax Court of Canada, presenting an independent, impartial expert witness is frequently decisive60.

System-Level Integration Uncertainty in Software and AI (DAZZM Inc., 6379249 Canada Inc.): While routine software development, API integration, and cloud configuration are excluded (C.W. Agencies), integrating multiple frameworks, open-source libraries, or AI/ML retrieval layers where conflicting architectural constraints (e.g., real-time latency, state synchronization, or unpredictable model behaviour) cannot be resolved by standard documentation creates valid system-level technological uncertainty58.

Iterative Hypothesis Analysis vs. Trial-and-Error (Joel Theatrical Rigging, Canafric, National R&D): Formulating a hypothesis (Question 2) is insufficient on its own (National R&D)66. To distinguish a systematic investigation (Question 3) from ineligible trial-and-error, the claimant must demonstrate that when an experiment failed, the team analysed why it failed scientifically or technologically and used that causal conclusion to modify the next hypothesis (Canafric)21. While contemporaneous documentation (Question 5) remains the primary evidentiary standard—and substantially reconstructed after-the-fact records risk claim denial (DAZZM Inc.)—the courts consistently apply RIS-Christie to accept credible, factually detailed oral testimony paired with authentic project artifacts8.
